topic: Eigenvalues of 2x2 Matrices: The DNA of Linear Transformations
target_audience: Undergraduate students in STEM fields (Mathematics, Physics, Engineering)

sections.title: Prerequisite & The Core Intuition
sections.content: Start by reviewing a 2x2 matrix as a 'transformer' of 2D space. Introduce 'Leo the Linear Cat,' a character drawn on a 2D grid. When we multiply the grid by a matrix, Leo gets stretched or squashed. Explain that while most points on Leo move to brand new directions, certain 'special' directions stay fixed along their original lines.
sections.example: Visualize Leo the Cat on a grid. Apply a transformation where he is stretched horizontally by 2. His whiskers on the x-axis stay on the x-axis (eigen-direction), while whiskers at 45 degrees tilt toward the horizontal.

sections.title: Defining the Eigen-Relationship
sections.content: Introduce the fundamental equation: Av = λv. Explain that 'A' is the matrix, 'v' is the eigenvector (the direction that doesn't change), and 'λ' (lambda) is the eigenvalue (the scale factor). Emphasize that in this specific direction, matrix multiplication simplifies to simple scalar multiplication.
sections.example: If A maps a vector v to 3v, then λ = 3. This means the 'DNA' of this transformation in that direction is a growth factor of 3.

sections.title: The Characteristic Equation (The Math Tool)
sections.content: Transition from geometry to algebra. To solve Av = λv, we rewrite it as (A - λI)v = 0. Explain that for a non-zero vector 'v' to exist, the matrix (A - λI) must be 'singular,' meaning its determinant must be zero. This leads to the characteristic equation: det(A - λI) = 0.
sections.example: Show a 2x2 matrix with 'λ' subtracted from the top-left and bottom-right diagonal elements, preparing it for the determinant calculation.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Calculation Example
sections.content: Walk through a concrete calculation using a 2x2 matrix. Show the expansion of the determinant into a quadratic equation (the characteristic polynomial) and solve for λ using factoring or the quadratic formula.
sections.example: Matrix A = [[4, 1], [2, 3]]. Calculation: det([[4-λ, 1], [2, 3-λ]]) = (4-λ)(3-λ) - 2 = λ² - 7λ + 10 = 0. Solving (λ-5)(λ-2)=0 gives eigenvalues λ₁=5 and λ₂=2.

sections.title: Visualizing the Resulting Transformation
sections.content: Connect the math back to Leo the Cat. Explain what the specific eigenvalues mean for the shape. If λ > 1, space expands; if 0 < λ < 1, space compresses; if λ is negative, space flips.
sections.example: Animate Leo being stretched 5 times longer along one diagonal (λ=5) and 2 times longer along another (λ=2). This gives a complete 'physical profile' of how the matrix A behaves.

sections.title: Summary & Application
sections.content: Wrap up by highlighting that eigenvalues are used in everything from Google's PageRank algorithm to analyzing the vibration of bridge cables. Reinforce that eigenvalues represent the 'scaling power' of a transformation.
sections.example: A bridge (device) vibrating: its 'natural frequencies' are determined by the eigenvalues of its structural matrix. High eigenvalue = high frequency vibration.
